data.title: Vyšný Kubín – Tupá skala, a Lusatian hillfort in the Orava region
data.excerpt: The hillfort of Tupá skala north of Vyšný Kubín rises 300 m above its surroundings; on the south its plateau of about 4 ha breaks off in rock faces 40–50 m deep, while the accessible northern side is barred by an earthen rampart which from below reaches 10 m and more. It was built by the people of the Orava group of the Lusatian culture, and a settlement of more than 20 hectares lay beneath it.

children.text: The hillfort of Tupá skala lies north of the village of Vyšný Kubín. It is a prominent elevation (relative height 300 m). The northern side of Tupá skala, with an area of about 4 ha, slopes gently, while the southern one ends abruptly in rock faces 40–50 m deep. From the north, that is from the accessible and strategically particularly sensitive side, the settlement area is barred by an earthen rampart in which two gateways survive. Originally there was only one here, in the north-eastern part of the fortification. The second was created in the modern period.
The hillfort was built and used by the
people of the Lusatian culture
in the Final Bronze Age and at the beginning of the Hallstatt period. This was a distinct branch of the Lusatian culture, the so-called
Orava group of the Lusatian culture
, which has certain features of its own in comparison with the Lusatian culture in other regions.
This was a thoroughly fortified
hillfort at the level of a tribal chieftain

with a warband. In this it differs substantially from other unfortified or open settlements. Craft production could be concentrated here, above all the working of metals and bone, but also pottery production and others, so that the settlement gradually became a centre of production, trade and administration for the territory belonging to it. In everyday life we may assume that it ensured the smooth running of work as well as the safety of the population in the surrounding area.
The hillfort also had a
settlement below it
, covering more than 20 ha. We may assume that there were enclosures, yards and even the dwellings of part of the farming or pastoral population.
The fortification
The fortified area is rectangular, with approximate
dimensions of 200 × 400 m

, its long axis oriented E – W. Tupá skala is mentioned as a settlement as early as 1859 by Michal Kubínyi (Prässburger Zeitung 13. 2. 1859), who owned a whole collection of bronze antiquities from his land here. The finds from Tupá skala were later reassessed and classified by J. Eisner and V. Budinský-Krička. In the 1960s and 1970s an archaeological excavation led by P. Čaplovič took place here. It turned out that settlement features stood over almost the whole area of Tupá skala.
The core of the hillfort’s defences rested on the massive mound of an earthen
rampart, which from the lower side sometimes reaches a height of 10 m and more

. The material for heaping it up comes from the immediate surroundings and is bound together with irregularly placed stones. Only in the uppermost parts does stone walling occur, faced on the outer side. No traces of a timber ramp have survived. It may, however, have been replaced by a ramp of earth and stone, levelled towards the settlement. On it hearths, ash, bones and sherds were recorded, and it was clearly visible in the section through the earthen rampart. This approach ramp of heaped stones, faced on the outer side as well and covered by a hardened layer of earth, was supplemented in the area of the stone walling by a timber palisade. The palisade may have been made of round timber, laid in the manner of a log structure.

children.text: Later the earthen rampart was heightened by more than 200 cm. Along its whole length, in a span of 4 and 7 m, stone walling was built in three rows, bound with timber and filled in with earth. On this raised base a new log structure was built, anchored also to massive posts set in places alongside it and elsewhere directly in the stone wall. The crest of the rampart now consisted of a 4 m wide step with a view over the surroundings and a 3 m wide lower step for handling things, or a space for bringing up supplies, all covered by a common roof sloping towards the settlement.
An
entrance gateway

was set into the body of the rampart in the north-eastern part. This gateway has a passage raised by more than 1 m with large sandstone blocks, which originally bound the rampart mound around the entrance and the gate like a revetment.
The internal buildings

All the settlement features that stood inside the hillfort were separated from the inner side of the body of the rampart by a stone wall. The space between them was a strategic thoroughfare in times of danger and, judging by the sherds of storage vessels, could also have served to hold a supply of water as an emergency fire reserve.

children.text: If we sum up the insights into the layout of the settlement, we can distinguish above all its fortification structures – the covered timber palisade – and then the dwelling and production features. Two phases in the construction of the palisade indicate its development, and the remains of dry-laid stone walling reveal that this really was a massively fortified hillfort.
The overall layout of the settlement is reflected in the dwelling and production features arranged in rows.
The features for preparing food

had, besides a hearth with a small post hole, supplies of food nearby as well, above all grain, pulses and meat. They were usually plastered with clay and oriented to the south. Alternating between the dwellings were
production features
, characterised by high-temperature hearths, vessels sunk into the floor and a different interior arrangement. One of the features found was a
smithy or casting workshop

for repairing working and fighting equipment. Between the rows of these features ran passages in the manner of streets following the line of the rampart. The number of features built in this way over the area of the settlement can be estimated at more than 300, if we disregard the other areas serving ancillary, technical, communication and social purposes. It is above all in the western, lowest part that the focus of these installations can be assumed.
Pottery
The oldest pottery on the settlement is represented by grooved and
graphite-coated Lusatian sherds
, found in the lower layers of the settlement features and in the fill of the defensive earthen rampart. Of the younger decorated pottery there are sherds
incised in the form of a conifer twig or of bundles of grooves
. A frequent form are handleless
undecorated pots
with round as well as elongated knobs below the rim. A distinct group of pottery on the settlement is formed by
large storage vessels,
placed partly in the features and partly in the communication space. Some storage vessels were not sunk into the floor.
The storage vessels placed outside had larger bases and more massive walls and resembled sack-shaped vessels with a knobbly surface. They could have served
to hold a supply of water

, while the storage vessels inside the features, with small bases, were used for storing food. Most of them had two or four strap handles and two or four tongue-shaped lugs in the lower half. These had a stabilising function and made it possible to carry or otherwise move the storage vessels.
Among the pottery products there are also numerous
spindle whorls
of discoid or conical shape,
loom weights
and stone
grinders
. Of stone there were also elongated whetstones with a drilled hole. Used on the settlement were
bone awls, smoothers and antler mallets
. Perhaps a
whistle
is what a bone tube decorated with rings on its surface may have been.
Metal
Of the metal objects, the most numerous are
pins with cruciform heads,
the so-called Orava type, triangular sheet-metal plates and a fragment of a
drum-shaped Hallstatt brooch
. Further finds were a
bronze chisel, a pin, a fragment of a bracelet, a spiral tube and a sheet-metal boss
with bent-over ends. From the military equipment, part of a
bronze shield fitting
was found, together with 8 three-sided, 1 two-sided and 2 bone
arrowheads.
Finally there are
grains
of cereals, with grains of millet, peas and broad beans. Grinding querns for processing grain were not lacking either.
On the whole, the assemblage of finds from Tupá skala does not depart from the framework of Hallstatt production on other settlements of this period.

After the destruction of the Hallstatt fortified settlement on Tupá skala, life moved to Ostrá skala, where a smaller settlement already existed in the Hallstatt period; it was disturbed by later interventions, and therefore the individual remains (pottery) are found in a secondary position.
